<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:2.1}
For every \(j\geq 1\) and \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\)
\begin{equation}
\left|(j + 1)^{i\tau} - j^{i\tau}\right|\leq |\tau |\log \left(1 + \frac{1}{j}\right)\leq \frac{|\tau|}{j}. \tag{8}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\| Q_{\tau}\| \leq |\tau |. \tag{9}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Factoring out \(j^{i\tau}\) whose modulus is one gives
\[
(j + 1)^{i\tau} - j^{i\tau} = j^{i\tau}\left[\exp \left(i\tau \log \left(1 + \frac{1}{j}\right)\right) - 1\right].
\]
Since \(|e^{ix} - 1|\leq |x|\) for real \(x\), the first inequality follows. The second inequality is the elementary bound \(\log (1 + x)\leq x\) for \(x\geq 0\). Multiplying by \(j\) gives (9).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:2.2}
For every \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\), the operator \(T_{\tau}\) defined by (7) is bounded on \(H^{2}\) and
\begin{equation}
\| T_{\tau}\| \leq 1 + 2|\tau |. \tag{10}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since \(D_{\tau}\) is unitary, by (6) and Lemma \ref{lem:2.1} we get
\[
\| \mathcal{C}Q_{\tau}\| \leq \| \mathcal{C}\| \| Q_{\tau}\| \leq 2|\tau |
\]
and therefore
$
\| T_{\tau}\| \leq \| D_{\tau}\| +\| \mathcal{C}Q_{\tau}\| \leq 1 + 2|\tau |.
$
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:3.2}
The family \((T_{\tau})_{\tau \in \mathbb{R}}\) is a one-parameter group of bounded invertible operators:
\begin{equation}
T_{\tau}T_{\sigma} = T_{\tau +\sigma},\qquad T_{0} = I,\qquad T_{\tau}^{-1} = T_{-\tau}. \tag{14}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Using (13) twice we get
\[
\Delta T_{\tau}T_{\sigma} = D_{\tau}\Delta T_{\sigma} = D_{\tau}D_{\sigma}\Delta = D_{\tau +\sigma}\Delta = \Delta T_{\tau +\sigma}.
\]
Since \(\Delta\) is injective we get \(T_{\tau}T_{\sigma} = T_{\tau +\sigma}\). The rest follow by taking \(\sigma = 0\) and \(\sigma = -\tau\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:4.1}
For \(g=\sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}b_{j}e_{j} \in H^2\),
\begin{equation}
(T_{\tau}^{*}g)_{0} = b_{0}, \tag{17}
\end{equation}
and, for every \(j \geq 1\),
\begin{equation}
(T_{\tau}^{*}g)_{j} = (j + 1)^{-i\tau}B_{j} - j^{-i\tau}B_{j - 1}. \tag{18}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From (4) and the definition of \(Q_{\tau}\), we have
\[
(T_{\tau}^{*}g)_{j} = (j + 1)^{-i\tau}b_{j} + ((j + 1)^{-i\tau} - j^{-i\tau})B_{j - 1},\qquad j\geq 1.
\]
Since \(b_{j} = B_{j} - B_{j - 1}\), this simplifies immediately to (18). The zeroth coordinate is (17) because \(D_{- \tau}e_{0} = e_{0}\) and \(Q_{\tau}^{*}e_{0} = 0\).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:5.1}
Let \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(\Re s > \frac{1}{2}\). Then
\begin{equation}
T_{\tau}^{*}k_{s} = \frac{\bar{s} + i\tau}{\bar{s}} k_{s - i\tau}. \tag{20}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The zeroth coefficient of \(T_{\tau}^{*}k_{s}\) is  \(- 1 / \bar{s}\) by (17) and (B). For \(j \geq 1\), insert (19) into (18):
\[
(T_{\tau}^{*}k_{s})_{j} = -\frac{1}{\bar{s}}\big((j + 1)^{1 - \bar{s} - i\tau} - j^{1 - \bar{s} - i\tau}\big).
\]
Since \(\overline{s - i\tau} = \bar{s} + i\tau\), multiplication of \(k_{s - i\tau}\) by \((\bar{s} + i\tau) / \bar{s}\) gives exactly these coefficients, including the zeroth one.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:6.1}
Fix \(\tau \in \mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\}\). Then the following are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] the Riemann hypothesis holds;
\item[(ii)] \(\overline{\mathcal{N}}\) is invariant under \(T_{\tau}\);
\item[(iii)] \(T_{\tau}h_{k}\in \overline{\mathcal{N}}\) for some integer \(k\geq 2\).
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if \(\rho\) is a zero of \(\zeta\) with \(\Re \rho >\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\zeta (\rho - i\tau)\neq 0\), then for every \(k\geq 2\)
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{dist}\big(T_{\tau}h_{k},\overline{\mathcal{N}}\big)\geq \frac{|\zeta(\rho - i\tau)||k^{1 - \rho + i\tau} - 1|}{|\rho|\|k_{\rho}\|} >0. \tag{21}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If RH holds, then (A) gives \(\overline{\mathcal{N}} = H^{2}\), so (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii). Since \(h_{k}\in \mathcal{N}\) for every \(k\geq 2\), (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) is immediate. Assume (iii), and suppose that RH is false. By the symmetry of the nontrivial zeros, there is a zero
\[
\rho = \beta +i\gamma ,\qquad \frac{1}{2} < \beta < 1,
\]
with \(\gamma >0\). Then \(k_{\rho}\in \mathcal{N}^{\perp}\) by (D). Since \(T_{\tau}h_{k}\in \overline{\mathcal{N}}\),
\[
0 = \langle T_{\tau}h_{k},k_{\rho}\rangle = \langle h_{k},T_{\tau}^{*}k_{\rho}\rangle .
\]
Using Theorem \ref{thm:5.1} and (C),
\begin{equation}
\langle T_{\tau}h_{k},k_{\rho}\rangle = -\frac{\zeta(\rho - i\tau)}{\rho}\big(k^{1 - \rho + i\tau} - 1\big). \tag{22}
\end{equation}
The second factor is nonzero, because
\[
|k^{1 - \rho +i\tau}| = k^{1 - \beta} > 1.
\]
Hence \(\zeta (\rho - i\tau) = 0\). Repeating the same argument with \(\rho - i\tau\), then \(\rho - 2i\tau\), and so on, gives
\begin{equation}
\zeta (\rho -i n\tau) = 0,\qquad n = 0,1,2,\ldots \tag{23}
\end{equation}
We now invoke Ingham's zero-density estimate. For \(\frac{1}{2} < \sigma < 1\), let
\[
N(\sigma ,T) = \# \{\rho ' = \beta ' + i\gamma ':\zeta (\rho ') = 0,\beta ' \geq \sigma ,0< \gamma ' \leq T\} ,
\]
counting multiplicity. Ingham proved \cite{Ingham40} that
\begin{equation}
N(\sigma ,T)\ll T^{\frac{3(1 - \sigma)}{2 - \sigma}}(\log T)^{5}. \tag{24}
\end{equation}
For every fixed \(\sigma > \frac{1}{2}\), the exponent $\frac{3(1 - \sigma)}{2 - \sigma}$ is strictly less than 1, and therefore
\begin{equation}
N(\sigma ,T) = o(T) \tag{25}
\end{equation}
since $(\log T)^k=o(T^\epsilon)$ for any fixed $k,\epsilon>0$. Choose \(\sigma\) with \(\frac{1}{2} < \sigma < \beta\). If \(\tau < 0\), the zeros in (23) themselves have positive ordinates growing in steps of \(|\tau |\). If \(\tau > 0\), their complex conjugates are zeros and, for all sufficiently large \(n\), have positive ordinates growing in steps of \(\tau\). In either case,
\[
N(\sigma ,T)\geq \frac{T}{|\tau|} +O(1),
\]
contradicting (25). Thus RH holds. It remains to prove the quantitative estimate (21). We use the elementary Hilbert-space bound
\[
g\in \mathcal{N}^{\perp}\quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mathrm{dist}(x,\overline{\mathcal{N}})\geq \frac{|\langle x,g\rangle|}{\|g\|}.
\]
Let \(\rho\) be as in the statement of the theorem. Then \(k_{\rho}\in \mathcal{N}^{\perp}\), so applying the bound with \(x = T_{\tau}h_{k}\) and \(g = k_{\rho}\), and then using (22), yields (21).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
